quoted_clause: So ~100 concurrent at peak ... ~2,000 registered users (an illustrative ~100 active users, not a simultaneous-request count; arrival rate and execution occupancy are separate quantities in Chapter 4) ... 40 rps × 8.6 s = 344 in-flight
observed: The canonical peak concurrency is stated as ~100 in Ch 23 but computed as 344 in Ch 24. With the canonical 8.6 s service time (which Ch 23 itself implies: ~25 ms/token × 300 output tokens ≈ 7.5 s decode plus prefill), a 40 rps peak requires 344 concurrent requests; 100 concurrent requests would sustain only 100/8.6 ≈ 11.6 rps. Ch 24 §1 additionally reinterprets the ~100 as 'active users, not a simultaneous-request count', contradicting Ch 23's derivation of it as concurrency.
correction: Fix the peak concurrency to 344 (or state the peak service time that makes 100 correct) and use one term for it across the book; if 'active users' and 'concurrent requests' are different quantities, name them differently in both chapters and state the mapping.
acceptance_test: Peak concurrency = peak rps × service time in every chapter; the '~100' figure appears with one consistent meaning, or is replaced.
verdict_evidence: chapter-23/chapter-23.md §8 reads 'an idealized 100% MFU ceiling (≤141 rps — 7B FP16, ~500 output tokens/request, H100)', then the worked example uses r = 50. Recomputed: 989e12/(2×7e9×500) = 141.3 rps (decode only); including the 500-token prefill the request rate is 989e12/(2×7e9×1000) = 70.6 rps at 100% MFU, ~24.7 rps at 35% MFU — so the stated 42–57 rps band and the r = 50 drain are ~2× optimistic.
fix_instruction: Add the qualifier and the total rate at chapter-23/chapter-23.md §8: 'decode-only ceiling; with the ~500-token prefill the total request rate is ~71 rps at 100% MFU (~21–28 rps at 30–40% MFU), so r = 50 in the worked example is an optimistic decode-only illustration — the measured per-host rate must replace it.'

observed: The customer's stated constraint is 'keep it on-prem if at all possible,' and Bound 5 explicitly allows cloud as a fallback if that preference yields. The mirror restatement upgrades this to a hard 'fully on-prem' requirement.
correction: Reword the mirror to 'on-prem preferred because it's regulated, with cloud only as a fallback if the on-prem preference cannot be met' or align Bound 5/Table 23-1 if the intent is truly mandatory.
acceptance_test: The mirrored requirement, Bound 5, and Table 23-1 all use the same strength (preference with fallback vs mandatory) for on-prem/cloud.
verdict_evidence: Lead: 'keep it on-prem if at all possible … '; Bound 5: 'on-prem is preferred "if at all possible," with cloud as the fallback if that preference yields'; the mirror restatement then hardens it to 'fully on-prem because it's regulated'.
fix_instruction: Mirror the preference, not a constraint: 'on-prem preferred (cloud only if that preference yields), because the data is regulated'.

quoted_clause: The vague ask collapsed into the exact canonical workload this book has architected end-to-end — a 70B-class model on an 8×H100 on-prem server becomes a candidate architecture whose memory fit can be derived
observed: The canonical architecture is described here as a single 8×H100 server, but the book's own canonical peak screens (Ch 24 §3.3 scope note) are 21 hosts (KV), 19–22 hosts (prefill), and a 32-host policy screen. One host cannot serve the canonical peak: 344 in-flight × 24.9 GB ≈ 8.6 TB of KV versus 640 GB of HBM.
correction: Rewrite as: the bounds select a 70B-class model served on 8×H100 hosts; the canonical fleet for this workload is ~21–32 such hosts (Ch 17/20), and the host is the unit of deployment, not the architecture.
acceptance_test: No chapter describes the canonical architecture as a single host; the host/fleet distinction is stated once and used consistently.
verdict_evidence: ch23 l.62 calls the workload 'a 70B-class model on an 8xH100 on-prem server', while ch24 l.91-102 puts the canonical peak at 21 hosts (KV) / 19-22 (prefill) / 32 (policy) and 344 x 24.9 GB ~ 8.57 TB of KV against 640 GB of HBM per host.
fix_instruction: Rewrite ch23 l.62 as '... a 70B-class model served on 8xH100 hosts - a ~21-32-host fleet at the canonical peak (Ch 17/20/24) - becomes a candidate architecture ...', keeping the host as the unit of deployment rather than the architecture itself.

quoted_clause: The worked-example interrogation, not a generic funnel: broad ask → five question gates (problem, success, data, constraints, what must be quantified) → quantified bounds → the decisions those bounds unlock. The full worked example (figure plus the §23.3 dialogue and Table 23-1) surfaces the six architectural numbers: the figure's boxes draw five of them (traffic & concurrency, token profile, SLO, ops/tier, TCO), and the worked example in §23.3 supplies the sixth (quality bar — Table 23-1, the "What's \"good\"?" row).
observed: The figure caption is extremely long (~100 words) and contains a detailed accounting of which of the six numbers the figure draws vs. which the dialogue supplies. This level of detail is better placed in the body text; the caption should state what the reader should learn from the figure.
correction: Shorten the caption to 1–2 sentences stating the figure's purpose (e.g., 'Interrogation sequence that converts a vague ask into quantified bounds; five of the six architectural numbers appear as gates, with the quality bar supplied by the §23.3 dialogue'). Move the out-of-scope list and figure-vs-dialogue accounting to a paragraph in the body text near the figure.
acceptance_test: The figure caption is ≤ 3 sentences and states what the reader should learn; detailed scoping appears in body prose.
verdict_evidence: ch23 l.111 lists 'either add capacity, add admission control, or scope the SLO to non-burst traffic' and then labels the chosen third option '(option a)'; no (a)/(b)/(c) enumeration exists in the chapter.
fix_instruction: Enumerate the three options as (a) add capacity, (b) add admission control, (c) scope the SLO to non-burst traffic and reference the chosen one as '(option c)'; or delete the label.

page_hint: Ch 23, §3 (mirror restatement) vs Bound 3 and Bound 5
quoted_clause: So to lock it: ~2,000 sales users, ~10 rps average / 40 peak, prompts with ~9,200-token retrieval context, answers starting under 2 s, quality judged on 50 of your real questions, fully on-prem because it's regulated
observed: The mirror restatement is not faithful to the conversation it mirrors: the lead said 'keep it on-prem if at all possible' (with cloud as fallback) but the mirror states 'fully on-prem because it's regulated' — upgrading a conditional preference into an absolute constraint; and Bound 3 was 'TTFT ≤ 2 s (p95)' but the mirror says only 'answers starting under 2 s', dropping the percentile the chapter says must be captured ('the percentile and the budget', §1 item 3).
correction: Mirror the conditional ('on-prem if at all possible, cloud fallback') and the percentile ('p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s'), and add a line where the lead confirms or corrects the restatement.
acceptance_test: The mirror text contains the 'if at all possible' condition and 'p95'; no bound is strengthened between the dialogue and the mirror.
verdict_evidence: ch23 l.55 lead: 'It's internal and regulated; keep it on-prem if at all possible' with cloud addressed in the question; l.48 Bound 3 is 'TTFT <= 2 s (p95)'; l.59 mirror states 'fully on-prem because it's regulated, answers starting under 2 s' and l.60 answers 'Yes - that's exactly it.'
fix_instruction: Restore the conditional and the percentile in the ch23 l.59 mirror ('on-prem if at all possible, cloud as fallback'; 'p95 TTFT <= 2 s') so no bound is strengthened between dialogue and restatement.

quoted_clause: → Bound 2: long ~9,200-token inputs with retrieval, ~300-token outputs.
observed: The dialogue never produces a token count. The lead says only 'they paste product specs and contracts, so the prompt can be lengthy — a few pages' (roughly 1–2K tokens), and the architect never asks for pages→tokens, for the retrieval chunk count, or for the output length. The canonical 9,200/300 figures appear as an assertion, which undercuts the chapter's claim that the conversation 'exposed the numbers'.
correction: Add the eliciting turns (pages per prompt, number of retrieved chunks, typical answer length) and show the conversion to tokens, so each of the six bounds traces to a specific line of dialogue.
acceptance_test: Each of the six bounds can be traced to a quoted customer line plus the architect's conversion step; no bound appears without a source in the dialogue.
verdict_evidence: ch23 l.42-44: the only token input is 'a few pages'; Bound 2 asserts 'long ~9,200-token inputs with retrieval, ~300-token outputs' - the output length is never mentioned by the lead and no pages->tokens conversion or retrieval-depth question appears.
fix_instruction: Add the eliciting turns (pages per prompt, retrieved-chunk count, typical answer length) plus an explicit pages->tokens conversion before Bound 2, or state that the token figures are imported from Ch 4 Table 4-2 rather than elicited.

quoted_clause: a 70B-class model on an 8×H100 on-prem server becomes a candidate architecture
observed: No reasoning step connects Bound 4 (a 50-question retrieval-QA benchmark) to a 70B-class model. The chapter's own §6 says 'quality feeds model selection (Ch 5)', but the worked example asserts the tier without the derivation, so the reader is shown the conclusion of the chapter's most important downstream decision with none of its reasoning.
correction: Either state that 70B is a candidate pending the 50-question benchmark (with the selection rule from Ch 5 named), or add the short derivation that maps the quality bar to a tier.
acceptance_test: The model-size statement in §3 cites the quality bound and the selection rule that produced it.
verdict_evidence: ch23 l.62 asserts the 70B tier with no criterion while l.94 says 'quality feeds model selection (Ch 5)'; Bound 4 (the 50-question retrieval-QA set) is the only quality input and no evaluation result or Ch 5 selection rule is invoked.
fix_instruction: At ch23 l.62, present 70B as the candidate tier the quality bound selects, pending the 50-question benchmark, and name the Ch 5 selection rule rather than asserting the tier.

quoted_clause: in this scenario the architect judges 7B-class to be the smallest tier that clears the resolution bar, which the pilot is there to confirm; the short ~500-token tickets are why 7B rather than 70B is judged sufficient
observed: The stated reason for choosing 7B is wrong: short context constrains KV footprint and memory, not ticket-resolution capability. Context length and capability are independent axes, and the chapter's own §6 says quality (not tokens) feeds model selection. The parenthetical also contradicts itself — the pilot is what confirms the resolution bar, so the bar cannot already be 'cleared'.
correction: Base the tier on the resolution benchmark (pilot on 5% of tickets, with a stated pass criterion), and note separately that short tickets keep KV footprint small enough for a single GPU — a memory argument, not a capability one.
acceptance_test: The tier choice cites a capability criterion and a pending measurement; no capability claim is derived from context length.
verdict_evidence: ch23 l.109 justifies the tier by length ('the short ~500-token tickets are why 7B rather than 70B is judged sufficient'), a memory argument, while the same clause says the resolution bar is 'what the pilot is there to confirm'.
fix_instruction: In ch23 l.109, base the tier on the resolution benchmark with a stated pass criterion and move the length point to memory ('short tickets keep KV footprint small'), dropping the claim that the resolution bar is already cleared.

quoted_clause: the 3 s SLO scoped to non-burst traffic, the burst served under the queue-and-drain degraded mode — and the architect is already architecting, not guessing
observed: The mini-case's most consequential decision — narrowing the customer's stated 3 s SLO to exclude bursts — is never mirrored back to the customer or confirmed, which is the exact discipline the chapter teaches in §2 ('The mirror test ... The restatement is where scope actually gets locked') and §5 ('Accepting aspirations as SLOs ... Write the contract'). The chapter's flagship example ends by violating its own rule.
correction: Add the mirror-and-confirm turn for the degraded-mode SLO (with a number, e.g., a separate burst SLO and an admission-control rule), or explicitly frame the scoping as an escalation the customer must approve.
acceptance_test: Every SLO change in the mini-case is mirrored and confirmed in the text; the mini-case ends with an explicit customer agreement.
verdict_evidence: ch23 l.109 mirrors 'resolving baseline tickets under 3 s', l.111 then narrows the 3 s SLO to non-burst traffic, and l.113 closes with no customer confirmation and no degraded-mode SLO value - against l.25 ('The restatement is where scope actually gets locked').
fix_instruction: Add a closing mirror-and-confirm turn to ch23 §8 carrying the burst/degraded-mode SLO value and the admission-control rule, approved by the customer.
